processed_notes.note_text:
Work/Life Balance and Meeting Attendance
• Struggles with attending required meetings due to work schedule.
  ◦ Has not had a day off since last Monday; works every Sunday, missing church and family time.
• Feels tired, unable to exercise or eat properly; relies on unhealthy food from Lizard’s Thicket.
• Upcoming Friday and Saturday off planned for rest and exercise.
• Acknowledges current stress is positive but recognizes risk of burnout.

Managing Overwhelm and Frustration
• Finds current workload overwhelming but not negative; sees it as growth.
• Believes juggling responsibilities will help long-term resilience.
• Identifies lack of sleep, exercise, and nutrition as early warning signs for frustration and relapse.
• Plans to accept current situation for next six weeks until Turn 90 ends.

Family Connections and Internal Struggles
• Wants to improve communication with his mom; feels isolated despite outward appearance.
• Struggles with post-prison adjustment and sorting through personal issues.
• Unsure how much to ask for help; feels pressure to handle things independently.
• Recognizes responsibility is new and challenging.

Positive Isolation and Avoiding Old Patterns
• Emphasizes importance of “positive isolation”—structured environment (e.g., Oxford House) with accountability.
• Avoids reconnecting with old friends to prevent relapse into negative behaviors.
• Boredom identified as a major trigger for past negative behaviors.
• Prefers to stay busy with work and programs to avoid idle time.

Oxford House Dynamics and Accountability
• On $175/week contract at Oxford House; feels it was imposed prematurely.
• Frustrated by lack of accountability for missed chapter meetings and household responsibilities.
• Hesitant to “snitch” but dislikes enabling rule-breaking.
• Considers holding a group meeting to improve communication and accountability.
• Discusses cultural shift from “don’t say anything” to understanding that people are responsible for their own actions.

Self-Talk and “I” Statements
• Works on using “I” statements to reinforce positive behaviors and avoid deflecting responsibility.
  ◦ Examples: “I don’t ever want to go back to prison,” “I want to do the right thing,” “I need to keep a structured environment,” “I like being responsible.”
• Feels lack of broader family support; only in contact with his mom.
• Adoption background discussed; no significant emotional baggage from it.

Leadership and House Culture
• Declined offer to be house president due to current commitments.
• Recognizes need for leadership and accountability in the house.
• Concerned about divisiveness and unchecked behaviors among housemates.
• Suggests more proactive group communication and involvement with house management.

External Support and Resources
• Offered connection to Chris Cherry, a recovery professional familiar with Oxford House dynamics.
• Encouraged to seek advice from experienced individuals for handling house issues.
• Discusses the importance of not enabling negative behaviors for the sake of house culture.

Therapeutic Activities and Addiction Replacement
• Knitting hats as a therapeutic, positive addiction; finds it calming and productive.
• Discusses concept of replacing negative addictions with positive ones (e.g., fitness, knitting).
• Misses regular exercise; identifies it as a key part of his well-being.

Reintegrating Fitness and Healthy Habits
• Struggles to maintain fitness routine due to work hours.
• Brainstorms ways to incorporate exercise, such as early morning jogs or lunchtime workouts.
• Considers meal prepping and using breaks for short workouts to improve mental health.

Career Planning and CDL Progress
• Interested in pursuing a CDL for truck driving; enjoys driving and sees it as stable income.
• Has all necessary documents except for a suspended license due to unresolved ticket in North Carolina.
• Needs to pay $65 reinstatement fee; no outstanding ticket to pay.
• Previously attempted to enroll in Road Master Trucking and SC Works but lacked funds.

Next Steps for CDL and Employment
• Will explore multiple CDL training options, including Knight’s Trucking (potential paid training) and other local schools.
• Encouraged to use Skillcat platform for CDL classes.
• Offered legal assistance if license issues become more complex.
• Open to relocation for job opportunities in Charleston or Spartanburg if needed.

Action Items and Follow-Up
• Plans to pay $65 fee to reinstate license.
• Will consider all CDL training options and choose best fit.
• Will try to reconnect with family, maintain structured environment, and use “I” statements.
• Will attempt to integrate exercise into daily routine.
• May hold a group meeting to address house accountability.
• Will be connected to Chris Cherry if desired for additional support.
• Will follow up with Will as requested at the end of the session.

**Session Context and Purpose**
- **Presenting Problem**: The client is seeking vocational exploration and placement support, addressing an arm issue, health/insurance barriers, transportation logistics, and credentialing needs. They express openness to multiple work pathways (including trucking) and interest in program structure, while navigating past rehab history and current housing/parole considerations.
- **Reason for Session**: Intake/informational meeting to outline the program, clarify how it integrates with Vocational Rehabilitation, discuss eligibility, logistics (transportation, waitlist), and co-create a plan for next steps (resume support, certifications, scheduling).
- **Stated Goals**: - Keep options open for employment opportunities and training. - Obtain medical/insurance guidance for the arm issue. - Explore and potentially enroll in the program; pursue OSHA certification and job skills. - Leverage Voc Rehab resources in conjunction with the program. - Develop a resume and prepare for job placement, aiming toward long-term goals such as trucking.

### **Key Themes and Emotional Tone**
**Main Topics Discussed**:
- Theme 1: Program structure and inter-agency coordination. The facilitator explains the Columbia-based program with four daily classes (CBT, job skills, computer lab/OSHA certification, and application of skills to work) from 9 to 3, plus the emphasis on frustration management and long-term employability. The potential synergy with Voc Rehab is highlighted.
- Theme 2: Barriers and logistics. The client discusses an unresolved arm issue, lack of insurance, transportation challenges, a waiting list, and the need to pass drug tests for program eligibility. Housing stability (Oxford House) and parole considerations are also noted.
- Theme 3: Motivation, resilience, and identity. The client articulates a trucking-family connection, desire to work, willingness to bus/train commute, and willingness to persist through discomfort. There is a focus on self-efficacy and building a new work-identity through skill-building and consistent engagement.

**Emotional Expression and Observations**:
- Dominant emotional states: Determination and pragmatism, with moments of concern about health care access and program logistics. Occasional frustration about systemic barriers (e.g., waitlists, car access). Hopeful about leveraging multiple resources.
- Patterns of emotional intensity shifts: From uncertainty about where to start to proactive planning (resume work, transportation plan, certifications) and reassurance about program structure.
- **Critical Moments**:
- Tension Points: Unclear medical status of arm and access to insurance; transportation feasibility to attend 9–3 schedule; waiting list length and time to start. Drug-testing policy adds another layer of potential barrier.
- Breakthroughs: Recognition of the complementary roles of programs (our CBT-focused program and Voc Rehab) and commitment to active steps (resume, OSH certification, job search). Willingness to use available transportation options and to adapt to a 9–3 daily schedule.
- Regression Points: Momentary confusion about which office/which staff to reference, resolved through clarification and moving forward.

### **Personal Content and Significant Events**
**Shared Personal Stories**:
- Significant memory or experience 1: The client notes a trucking heritage in the biological family, framing the trucking goal as something “in my DNA.” This connects identity to career aspirations.
- Significant memory or experience 2: Past rehab experiences and the impact of health issues (arm condition) on work plans; ongoing navigation of housing and parole contexts.

**Relationships and Conflicts**:
- Key relationships: Program staff (this session), Vocational Rehabilitation resources, parole system (drug testing requirements), housing (Oxford House), and family/financial supporters who might assist with transportation or car access.
- Conflicts or tensions: Balancing health issues with employment goals; coordinating multiple programs with different eligibility and funding criteria; transportation and time management constraints.

**Notable Expressions**:
- Key Phrases:
- "I want to keep my mind open to different things"
- "I don't want to hurt myself any more than I already have"
- "we complement each other" (between our program and Voc Rehab)
- "the bar is set very low now" (emphasis on simple, clear benchmarks)
- "manage frustration" (topic of this morning’s discussion)
- "it's in my DNA" (trucking heritage)
- Metaphors Used:
- DNA reference to family/cultural heritage shaping career aims.
- Framing the program’s requirements as approachable with a “low” bar to begin with, then building toward real-world demands.

**Core Themes Involved**:
- □ Attachment □ Trauma □ Loss □ Identity □ Boundaries □ Self-image
- How these themes are addressed: The client’s exploration of career identity (trucking heritage) signals identity work and self-image in relation to work. The conversation touches on trauma-related aspects (past addiction and parole) in the context of current abstinence and reintegration. Boundaries emerge in navigating program expectations, transportation, and family support. Attachment considerations surface in how the client engages with support systems (Voc Rehab, housing, parole) to maintain stability and progress.

### **Patterns, Beliefs, and Coping Mechanisms**
**Repetitive Patterns**:
- Behavioral Patterns: Willingness to engage with new programs, consistent attention to transportation and scheduling, readiness to complete paperwork (resume worksheet).
- Thought Patterns: Openness to multiple options, belief in gradual skill-building through CBT and job skills, and recognition that frustration management is essential to persistence.

**Belief Systems**:
- **Limiting Beliefs**: Potential doubts about how quickly they can start or access resources due to waitlists and logistical barriers; concern about health insurance coverage for arm care.
- **Empowering Beliefs**: Confidence in heritage driving motivation, belief that multiple programs can be synergistic, and trust in structured processes (CBT, resume support, OSHA certification) to enable employment.

**Coping Mechanisms**:
- Problem-solving orientation (mapping transportation, seeking scheduling flexibility).
- Resource-seeking (resume help, OSH certification, computer lab access, staff support).
- Realistic planning (accepting wait times, leveraging bus routes, transparency about program limitations).

### **Insights, Reflections, and Breakthroughs**
**Emerging Insights**:
- Recognition that CBT-based thinking can shape workplace behavior and frustration tolerance, supporting long-term goal achievement.
- Understanding that Voc Rehab can complement the program by addressing concrete needs (transportation, clothing, certification funding).
- Clarity about transportation as a central logistical challenge and a concrete area to problem-solve.

**Emotional Processing Moments**:
- Open acknowledgment of past patterns (prison/involvement with substances) and current commitment to abstinence and compliance with program requirements (drug tests).
- Willingness to adopt a structured routine (9–3 schedule) and to manage the required discipline (being on time, staying off the phone, completing homework).

**Shifts in Perspective**:
- From viewing programs in isolation to seeing a coordinated system of supports (internal CBT tools plus external resources like Voc Rehab).
- From focusing on barriers alone to actively planning practical steps (resume worksheet, transportation plan, OSH certification) and accepting waiting periods as a reality of program access.

### **Therapeutic Interventions and Methods**
**Techniques Employed**:
- Psychoeducation on CBT: explanation of the thinking-feeling-behavior cycle and how beliefs shape actions.
- Program orientation: outlining class structure, times, and concrete skills (OSHA, resume-building).
- Resource coordination: discussing Voc Rehab alignment, transportation logistics, and financial supports (boots, certifications).
- Reality-testing and transparency: clear discussion of waitlists, staffing issues, and eligibility requirements (drug testing).

**Client Responses**:
- **Openness**: Engages actively, asks clarifying questions, agrees to resume assistance, and expresses willingness to adapt to transportation needs.
- **Resistance/Avoidance**: Minimal; initial confusion about office location resolved quickly.
- **Emotional Reactions**: Mild frustration about systemic barriers; positive engagement with structure and transparent communication; relief at practical support (resume help, certificate opportunities).

### **Concerns, Challenges, and Needs**
**Expressed Concerns**:
- Medical: unresolved arm issue and lack of health coverage/insurance; need for medical assessment and ongoing care.
- Financial/Logistical: transportation to the program, wait times, and the potential need for external funding or support for work-related costs.
- Legal/Compliance: parole drug testing requirements; ensuring eligibility and avoiding program disqualification due to testing policies.
- System Navigation: understanding which offices/staff are involved and how to access supports (e.g., receiving documents, sending resumes).

**Emotional Barriers**:
- Uncertainty about how soon engagement can begin due to waitlists and staffing.
- Anxiety about meeting program prerequisites (drug testing) and logistics (transportation, housing stability).

**Identified Needs**:
- Medical evaluation and insurance assistance for the arm injury.
- Clear, actionable plan to address transportation (consistent means to attend daily sessions).
- Resume development and job-readiness support; help applying for OSHA certification.
- Ongoing communication channel (text/phone) given staffing realities and waitlists.
- Transparent timeline for eligibility and start date; status updates on waitlist position.

### **Agreements, Exercises, and Next Steps**
**Assigned Homework**:
- Complete the resume worksheet; gather and submit relevant information (via text or email). The facilitator will assist in formatting and can fax or email the document back if needed.

**Therapeutic Goals**:
- Short-term Goals: - Clarify medical and insurance needs for arm injury. - Determine transportation plan to attend the program consistently. - Complete resume worksheet and establish contact for ongoing updates. - Confirm eligibility and next steps despite the waiting list.
- Long-term Goals: - Complete the CBT and job skills components; obtain OSHA certification; secure employment in a field aligned with trucking / logistics. - Build sustainable routines and coping strategies to manage frustration and maintain engagement.

**Follow-up Plan**:
- Next Session Focus: - Review medical/insurance status and arm care plan. - Confirm transportation arrangements and address any barriers. - Update on waiting list status and potential start date. - Finalize resume and begin OSH certification steps.
- Scheduling: Next contact via text; ongoing communication to monitor waiting list progression and eligibility updates.
